rule: bad: this rule can never fire — the participle "landing on lanterns" is packed into the condition as an invented landing event that no actual landing recorded from another sentence can ever match, so nothing about threads is ever derived from it. Rewrite as "When a nightmoth lands on a lantern, the nightmoth leaves silken threads on the lantern.": one finite clause per event with explicit subjects. Your own first text is worded that way and it fires.
texts: good. fires on any landing, with the moth, the lantern, the leaving, the threads and their location on the lantern all covered.
good. fires whenever a moth is resting on a lantern, with the shedding, the threads and the lantern as destination all covered.

mixed: the rule fires, but "the undersides of nightmoths" becomes one single set of undersides recorded as a part of the kind nightmoth rather than of any moth, so every thread is said to come from that same shared set. Rewrite as "Every silken thread comes from the underside of a nightmoth." so each thread gets its own moth and that moth's own underside.
